items.stem: Identify the term for the following: “Learning in which a neutral stimulus becomes associated with an unconditioned stimulus, so that it comes to produce a conditioned response”.
items.answer: Classical conditioning
items.markingKey: Classical conditioning: learning in which a neutral stimulus becomes associated with an unconditioned stimulus, so that it comes to produce a conditioned response. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): A phobia can develop after a single frightening experience. Reason (R): Classical conditioning can occur after one strong pairing of a neutral stimulus with an unpleasant event. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: One-trial learning explains rapid onset. [1]

items.stem: Use classical conditioning to explain how the boy in Saavedra and Silverman’s study developed his button phobia.
items.answer: Buttons (neutral stimulus) were paired with the shock and embarrassment of a bowl of buttons falling on him (unconditioned stimulus, producing distress); buttons became a conditioned stimulus that produced a conditioned response of distress and disgust.
items.markingKey: 1 mark NS → CS; 1 mark UCS/UCR; 1 mark CR [3]

items.stem: Priya, aged 10, from Bangkok, became very afraid of balloons after one burst loudly near her face at a party. She now leaves the room whenever she sees one. Explain why Priya continues to avoid balloons.
items.answer: Leaving the room reduces her anxiety, which negatively reinforces avoidance; she never learns that balloons are usually harmless, so the fear does not extinguish.
items.markingKey: 1 mark negative reinforcement; 1 mark no extinction [2]

items.stem: Priya, aged 10, from Mumbai, became very afraid of balloons after one burst loudly near her face at a party. She now leaves the room whenever she sees one. (a) Identify the neutral stimulus and the unconditioned stimulus. (b) Suggest how exposure could be used to help Priya.
items.answer: (a) Neutral stimulus: the balloon. Unconditioned stimulus: the loud bang near her face. (b) Build a hierarchy from pictures of balloons to holding an uninflated balloon to being near inflated balloons, moving up only when distress falls.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark hierarchy; 1 mark gradual exposure [2]

items.stem: What is meant by ‘classical conditioning’?
items.answer: Learning in which a neutral stimulus becomes associated with an unconditioned stimulus, so that it comes to produce a conditioned response.
items.markingKey: Classical conditioning: learning in which a neutral stimulus becomes associated with an unconditioned stimulus, so that it comes to produce a conditioned response. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Classical conditioning can explain why a phobia is maintained over time.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Classical conditioning explains acquisition; maintenance is often explained by negative reinforcement of avoidance (operant conditioning).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why disgust-based phobias may be harder to treat than fear-based phobias.
items.answer: Disgust appears to extinguish more slowly than fear during exposure, so a person may stop feeling afraid but still feel disgusted and continue avoiding the object.
items.markingKey: 1 mark disgust slower to extinguish; 1 mark consequence [2]

items.stem: “Saavedra and Silverman’s (2002) case study of a button phobia has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including self-report in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): The study suggests that when a phobia is based on disgust, imagery exposure targeting disgust can help where exposure alone is not enough. Strength (ethics): The boy received treatment that helped him, his parents consented, and his identity was protected. Weakness (generalisability): It is a case study of one 9-year-old boy with an unusual phobia, so the findings may not apply to other children or other phobias. Weakness (self-report): Ratings and reports came from the boy and his mother, so they may be affected by demand characteristics or a wish to show improvement. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Describe the treatment used by Saavedra and Silverman.
items.answer: Exposure-based CBT: the boy worked through a 12-step hierarchy of buttons with contingency management (praise and rewards for approaching), then imagery exposure in which he imagined disgusting button-related scenes, plus self-control strategies (coping thoughts); he rated distress and disgust throughout.
items.markingKey: 1 mark hierarchy/exposure; 1 mark reinforcement; 1 mark disgust imagery; 1 mark ratings [4]

items.stem: A clinic in Muscat compared distress ratings (0–8 feeling thermometer) after treatment for 6 children with phobias treated with exposure therapy and 6 children on a waiting list. Table: Distress rating (0–8) — Exposure therapy: 1, 4, 1, 3, 4, 3. Waiting list: 4, 6, 6, 5, 6, 5. (a) Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here. (b) The participants were people selected from a full list of residents of Muscat using a random number generator. Identify the sampling technique used and explain one weakness of it.
items.answer: (a) Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV. (b) Random sampling. Weakness: random selection does not guarantee a representative sample, especially when the sample is small, and some people may refuse.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2] (b) 1 mark: sampling technique; 1 mark: weakness explained [2]

items.stem: “Saavedra and Silverman’s (2002) case study of a button phobia has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including the case study method in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): The study suggests that when a phobia is based on disgust, imagery exposure targeting disgust can help where exposure alone is not enough. Strength (the case study method): Studying one boy in depth over time, with interviews, ratings and follow-up, gave detailed evidence about how the phobia developed and how disgust and distress changed during treatment. Weakness (self-report): Ratings and reports came from the boy and his mother, so they may be affected by demand characteristics or a wish to show improvement. Weakness (controls): Several treatment elements were combined and there was no control condition, so it is impossible to know which element caused the improvement. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Describe the results of Saavedra and Silverman’s study.
items.answer: Distress decreased during exposure with rewards, but disgust stayed higher until disgust-focused imagery was added; after treatment and at 6- and 12-month follow-up he no longer met the criteria for a phobia and could wear clothes with buttons.
items.markingKey: 1 mark distress fell; 1 mark disgust needed imagery; 1 mark follow-up [3]

items.stem: What is meant by ‘phobia’?
items.answer: An intense, irrational and persistent fear of a specific object or situation, leading to avoidance.
items.markingKey: Phobia: an intense, irrational and persistent fear of a specific object or situation, leading to avoidance. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: Outline one strength of Saavedra and Silverman’s (2002) case study of a button phobia that relates to ethics.
items.answer: The boy received treatment that helped him, his parents consented, and his identity was protected.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to ethics; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Saavedra and Silverman’s (2002) case study of a button phobia can be evaluated in terms of self-report. Explain one weakness of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: Ratings and reports came from the boy and his mother, so they may be affected by demand characteristics or a wish to show improvement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to self-report; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A therapist in Toronto is treating Sipho, a teenager with a fear of cockroaches that involves strong disgust. Explain why exposure alone might not be enough.
items.answer: Disgust may extinguish more slowly than fear, so Sipho could stop being afraid but still avoid cockroaches because of disgust.
items.markingKey: 1 mark disgust slower; 1 mark consequence [2]

items.stem: A clinic in Hanoi compared distress ratings (0–8 feeling thermometer) after treatment for 6 children with phobias treated with exposure therapy and 6 children on a waiting list. Table: Distress rating (0–8) — Exposure therapy: 3, 2, 4, 3, 2, 3. Waiting list: 6, 4, 4, 5, 5, 4. (a) Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place. (b) Calculate the median score for the exposure therapy condition.
items.answer: (a) Exposure therapy: 2.8; waiting list: 4.7. (b) 3
items.markingKey: (a) Exposure therapy: 17 ÷ 6 = 2.8; waiting list: 28 ÷ 6 = 4.7. 1 mark for each correct mean [2] (b) Ordered scores: 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4; median = 3. 1 mark: data ordered; 1 mark: correct median [2]

items.stem: Assess the view that phobias are best explained by classical conditioning.
items.answer: Arguments for: The button phobia began after a single unpleasant event when buttons fell on the boy, consistent with conditioning. Exposure therapy based on conditioning reduced his fear. Arguments against: Not everyone who has a bad experience develops a phobia, so individual factors matter. Disgust, a cognitive and emotional response, had to be treated separately. Biological preparedness may explain why some fears develop more easily. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “A stimulus that naturally produces a response without learning”?
items.answer: Unconditioned stimulus
items.markingKey: Unconditioned stimulus: a stimulus that naturally produces a response without learning. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A student writes: “Classical conditioning can explain why a phobia is maintained over time.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why disgust-based phobias may be harder to treat than fear-based phobias.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Classical conditioning explains acquisition; maintenance is often explained by negative reinforcement of avoidance (operant conditioning). (b) Disgust appears to extinguish more slowly than fear during exposure, so a person may stop feeling afraid but still feel disgusted and continue avoiding the object.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark disgust slower to extinguish; 1 mark consequence [2]

items.stem: Explain one weakness of Saavedra and Silverman’s (2002) case study of a button phobia in terms of self-report.
items.answer: Ratings and reports came from the boy and his mother, so they may be affected by demand characteristics or a wish to show improvement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to self-report; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Diego, aged 10, from Santiago, became very afraid of balloons after one burst loudly near her face at a party. She now leaves the room whenever she sees one. Suggest how exposure could be used to help Diego.
items.answer: Build a hierarchy from pictures of balloons to holding an uninflated balloon to being near inflated balloons, moving up only when distress falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark hierarchy; 1 mark gradual exposure [2]

items.stem: A clinic in Lagos compared distress ratings (0–8 feeling thermometer) after treatment for 6 children with phobias treated with exposure therapy and 6 children on a waiting list. Table: Distress rating (0–8) — Exposure therapy: 3, 2, 1, 0, 3, 3. Waiting list: 6, 6, 3, 5, 6, 7. Explain one ethical issue that the researcher should consider in this study.
items.answer: The waiting-list children should be offered treatment afterwards.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: ethical guideline named; 1 mark: applied to this study [2]

items.stem: Noah, aged 10, from Mexico City, became very afraid of balloons after one burst loudly near her face at a party. She now leaves the room whenever she sees one. (a) Identify the neutral stimulus and the unconditioned stimulus. (b) Explain why Noah continues to avoid balloons.
items.answer: (a) Neutral stimulus: the balloon. Unconditioned stimulus: the loud bang near her face. (b) Leaving the room reduces her anxiety, which negatively reinforces avoidance; she never learns that balloons are usually harmless, so the fear does not extinguish.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark negative reinforcement; 1 mark no extinction [2]

items.stem: ‘Case studies are the most useful way to study phobias.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: Arguments for: They allow rare phobias to be studied in depth, as Saavedra and Silverman did. Detailed treatment records help clinicians. Arguments against: Findings from one person may not generalise. There is no control group, so causes of improvement are unclear. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: How many steps were in the boy’s hierarchy?
items.markingKey: A 12-step stimulus hierarchy was used. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a stimulus hierarchy was used in this treatment. (b) Describe the results of Saavedra and Silverman’s study.
items.answer: (a) It allowed the boy to face buttons gradually, starting with the least distressing (large denim buttons) and moving to the most (small plastic buttons), so anxiety stayed manageable and could reduce at each step. (b) Distress decreased during exposure with rewards, but disgust stayed higher until disgust-focused imagery was added; after treatment and at 6- and 12-month follow-up he no longer met the criteria for a phobia and could wear clothes with buttons.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark graded; 1 mark manageable/extinction [2] (b) 1 mark distress fell; 1 mark disgust needed imagery; 1 mark follow-up [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “Saavedra and Silverman found that the boy’s disgust disappeared after the first session.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Describe the results of Saavedra and Silverman’s study.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Disgust was slower to change and needed imagery-based exposure. (b) Distress decreased during exposure with rewards, but disgust stayed higher until disgust-focused imagery was added; after treatment and at 6- and 12-month follow-up he no longer met the criteria for a phobia and could wear clothes with buttons.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark distress fell; 1 mark disgust needed imagery; 1 mark follow-up [3]

items.stem: A clinic in Auckland compared distress ratings (0–8 feeling thermometer) after treatment for 7 children with phobias treated with exposure therapy and 7 children on a waiting list. Table: Distress rating (0–8) — Exposure therapy: 4, 2, 2, 4, 3, 4, 3. Waiting list: 6, 7, 7, 8, 7, 4, 6. Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place.
items.answer: Exposure therapy: 3.1; waiting list: 6.4.
items.markingKey: Exposure therapy: 22 ÷ 7 = 3.1; waiting list: 45 ÷ 7 = 6.4. 1 mark for each correct mean [2]

items.stem: A clinic in Istanbul compared distress ratings (0–8 feeling thermometer) after treatment for 6 children with phobias treated with exposure therapy and 6 children on a waiting list. Table: Distress rating (0–8) — Exposure therapy: 3, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2. Waiting list: 6, 6, 3, 4, 4, 6. Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why.
items.answer: Children of similar age and phobia severity in both groups.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant control identified; 1 mark: explains how it would otherwise act as a confounding variable [2]

items.stem: Plan an interview to investigate how common disgust-based fears are among teenagers. Your plan must include: the sampling technique, ethical issues and one example question.
items.answer: Method: an interview. A structured or semi-structured interview with set questions asked in the same order; record and transcribe answers; train interviewers. Variables: topic: disgust-based fears; measure: ratings of disgust for objects and open answers. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Santiago, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Mei wants to find out how common disgust-based fears are among teenagers. Plan an interview to investigate this. Your plan must include: how the data will be analysed, the type of interview, the sampling technique and ethical issues. Then explain one weakness of your plan and how it could be overcome.
items.answer: Method: an interview. A structured or semi-structured interview with set questions asked in the same order; record and transcribe answers; train interviewers. Variables: topic: disgust-based fears; measure: ratings of disgust for objects and open answers. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Kuala Lumpur, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected. Weakness: for example a small or biased sample; overcome by a larger, more representative sample.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: What is meant by ‘unconditioned stimulus’?
items.answer: A stimulus that naturally produces a response without learning.
items.markingKey: Unconditioned stimulus: a stimulus that naturally produces a response without learning. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: Saavedra and Silverman’s (2002) case study of a button phobia can be evaluated in terms of generalisability. Explain one weakness of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: It is a case study of one 9-year-old boy with an unusual phobia, so the findings may not apply to other children or other phobias.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to generalisability; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Explain one strength of Saavedra and Silverman’s (2002) case study of a button phobia in terms of the case study method.
items.answer: Studying one boy in depth over time, with interviews, ratings and follow-up, gave detailed evidence about how the phobia developed and how disgust and distress changed during treatment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to the case study method; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Ana measured fear on a 0–8 feeling thermometer after eight weeks for children given exposure therapy or placed on a waiting list. Table: Distress rating (0–8) — Exposure therapy: 3, 2, 3, 5, 5, 3. Waiting list: 5, 5, 4, 5, 8, 5. Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results.
items.answer: The waiting list condition had a higher mean (5.3) than the exposure therapy condition (3.5), suggesting that exposure therapy reduces distress compared with no treatment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2]

items.stem: A therapist in Cape Town is treating Grace, a teenager with a fear of cockroaches that involves strong disgust. (a) Explain why exposure alone might not be enough. (b) Explain one reason why a treatment that worked for the boy in Saavedra and Silverman’s case may not work for Grace.
items.answer: (a) Disgust may extinguish more slowly than fear, so Grace could stop being afraid but still avoid cockroaches because of disgust. (b) The boy was a single case with a unique history; Grace’s phobia may have a different cause, and individual differences mean responses to treatment vary.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark disgust slower; 1 mark consequence [2] (b) 1 mark single case; 1 mark individual differences [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Lisbon is interested in whether gradual exposure reduces children’s fear of dogs. Plan a field experiment to test this. Your plan must include: the experimental design, how the dependent variable will be measured and the sampling technique.
items.answer: Method: a field experiment. Manipulate the IV in a natural everyday setting; participants may not know they are being studied; standardise as much of the procedure as possible. Variables: IV: gradual exposure or no exposure; DV: distress rating on a feeling thermometer. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Lisbon, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
